"Pursuant" as an adjective lives almost entirely inside one phrase: "pursuant to." Mastering that two-word phrase is all you need.

"Pursuant to" means in accordance with, following from, or as required or authorized by something. It tells you that an action, decision, or situation exists because of — and in direct obedience or response to — whatever comes right after those two words. That "whatever" is almost always a rule, law, contract, order, or request.

The simplest way to see it in action:

"Pursuant to the contract, payment is due on Friday."

This means: "In accordance with what the contract says — following its terms — payment is due on Friday." The contract is the source. The payment deadline obeys and flows directly from it.

Another example:

"Pursuant to your request, I have attached the report."

This means: "Following your request, and in direct response to it, here is the report." Your request is the source. The attached report is the action that follows from it.

While the core idea stays consistent, "pursuant to" carries slightly different flavors depending on context.

The most common use is "in accordance with / as required by" — when a law, regulation, or agreement is the governing source: "Pursuant to federal law, all employees must be paid minimum wage." Here, the law is the authority, and the requirement follows directly from it.

The second use is "following / in response to" — when an action is a direct follow-up to a request or prior event: "Pursuant to our last conversation, I have drafted the proposal." The conversation prompted the action; the proposal is its direct result.

A third, older and rarer use means "in pursuit of / for the purpose of achieving" something: "measures taken pursuant to peace." This means measures taken with the aim of bringing about peace. You'll rarely encounter this version in modern writing, but it's worth knowing.
How to recognize it and where you'll see it

"Pursuant" is a formal word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. It lives in legal documents, official letters, government notices, business contracts, and formal correspondence. When writing casually, people replace it with simpler alternatives: "as required by the contract," "following your request," "in line with the law." But in formal or legal writing, "pursuant to" is the standard go-to phrase, and you will see it constantly.

Technically, "pursuant" is an adjective because it modifies the subject of a sentence by describing its relationship to something else. In "actions taken pursuant to the agreement," the word "pursuant" describes the actions — it tells you their nature: that they follow from and comply with the agreement. However, in practice, the full phrase "pursuant to" behaves like a preposition — it connects what comes before it (an action or fact) to what comes after it (its source or basis). Don't lose sleep over the grammar label. What matters is how it functions: it links something to the rule, authority, or event that caused or governs it.

Because "pursuant" and "pursuit" share the same root, people sometimes mix up "pursuant to" with "in pursuit of." These are not the same thing in modern usage.

"He acted pursuant to the law" means he acted in accordance with the law — he followed it.

"He acted in pursuit of the criminal" means he chased the criminal.

In modern English, "pursuant to" almost never means physically chasing or hunting. It means following from, obeying, or acting in line with something.

Any time you see "pursuant to" in a sentence, try swapping it with "in accordance with" or "as required by." If the sentence still makes sense, you've read the word correctly. In the vast majority of cases, this substitution will work perfectly, and you'll know exactly what the sentence means.
